newsitem.title: UK: Europe crude outlook - Trapped bears take prices up.
newsitem.headline: Europe crude outlook - Trapped bears take prices up.

text.p: Dated Brent was likely to hold on to its recently improved values with traders expecting the North Sea benchmark to keep steady into the week as OPEC ministers gather for their Vienna meeting.
Nervous buying on Friday pushed Dated Brent higher and some traders put it at a notional Dec -35 cents a barrel this week, and possibly higher if last week's buying spree persists.
"Our view was always that Brent was going to trade at a 35 cent discount. Our view remains the same for next week," a Brent trader said Friday, reflecting on a 40 cent jump over the week.

"Margins have been outstanding and the impression was that there was a lot of crude. But it is reasonably cold and some thought that in the short-term nothing will change very much so people got very bearish and a lot of people have been cut short," he added.

OPEC ministers are expected to agree a rollover of the current 25.03 million barrels per day ceiling for another six months leaving a market that has been able to absorb much of the leakage from some producers without an adverse impact on prices.
CFD values for this week's dates indicated the market's belief of Brent's upward mobility.
This week's CFDs moved from a contango of 20 cents against January paper to a 25 cent backwardation late on Friday.

"This indicates a very nervous market because it has been such a massive move. Some shorts are nervous but are reluctant to cover on CFDs. They missed the boat and now they are nervous," the trader said.
Another trader said the sentiment could be transient with buyers trying to take advantage of low prices.
Ekofisk, which normally languishes at this time of year as refiners opt for gas oil grades, was snapped up on Friday. Its premium over Brent moved from three to 10 cents over the day.
"Some differentials are so low that people are trying to lock them in now," another wet trader said.
The big question was whether refineries would opt to see the year out with low inventories, as has been the recent trend, which could depress prices.
"It's typical of a depressed market, as people keep a low inventory that it goes down and down then everybody panics," another wet trader said.
In the Med, sour Urals was expected to maintain recent better values with fears of delays in the Black Sea underlined by the closure of Novorossiisk for bad weather.

West African crudes were also seen improving after December barrels began to shift. A trader for an oil company said U.S. clients may have to pay more for their barrels with the Med and the East absorbing more than their usual share of West African oil.
"There has been a good enough market in the East and the Med that they didn't have to go to the West but the arb is opening up now and the West will have to pay up," he said.
He added that it was now harder to predict where West African differentials were heading because the traditional relationships between various grades had broken up.
